Title: Assessing Knowledge and Risk Perception of Mosquitoes and Mosquito-Borne Viruses Among Medical Students in Cyprus: A Cross-Sectional MosquitoWise Study
Authors: Dali, A. M.; Vujicic, A.; Gato, D.; Volkan, E.
Abstract: BackgroundCyprus has transitioned into a high-alert zone for mosquito-borne viruses. This necessitates a proactive assessment of its future physicians. Following the 2022 re-establishment of Aedes aegypti in Larnaca and Aedes albopictus in Limassol, Cyprus, the island is now biologically primed for local outbreaks of dengue, Zika and chikungunya, alongside Culex-borne West Nile virus. This study assessed medical students knowledge and risk perception.  MethodsA cross-sectional online survey administered the validated MosquitoWise Health Belief Model instrument to undergraduate-entry and graduate-entry students at a university in Cyprus in mid-2026.  ResultsOf 1023 students, 119 responded (11.6%), with pre-clinical students overrepresented (p<0.001). Mean knowledge was 5.43/9, stronger on mosquito biology (72.5%) than virus knowledge (54.2%). Median severity was 6.00/7 against susceptibility 4.25/7. Knowledge differed by study stage (p<0.001), correlated with severity (rs = 0.399) but not susceptibility.  ConclusionsThis study establishes a critical baseline for pre-clinical medical students in Cyprus. Overall, participants performed better on mosquito biology when compared to mosquito-borne viruses and how they spread. Our findings highlight the value of integrating theoretical microbiology with clinical practice in medical education to enhance physicians preparedness for the changing landscape of newly emerging infections in Cyprus and across Europe as a whole.

Title: Rejecting Perfection, Valuing Imperfection in Perinatal Care: a Mixed-Methods Study of Responsive Practice Through The Five Misfits by Beatrice Alemagna
Abstract: Picture books are recognised within the medical humanities as narrative tools capable of supporting reflective practice, emotional awareness and professional development among healthcare practitioners. In perinatal care, where relational demands are high and emotional exposure is constant, they may help practitioners examine implicit professional models, including attitudes towards vulnerability, imperfection and paternalism. This mixed-methods study explored how 34 perinatal professionals attending a postgraduate training programme interpreted The Five Misfits by Beatrice Alemagna, and how engagement with its characters supported reflection on responsive models of care. Forum-based written reflections following a facilitated reading of the picture book were analysed through inductive thematic analysis; eight thematic dimensions relevant to responsive care were scored on a bipolar scale (-2 to +2), and character profiles were compared statistically and read alongside qualitative excerpts. Participants rejected a professional stance characterised by perfectionism and the imposition of solutions, associated with paternalism and with negative emotional responses (90%), while symbolic representations of imperfection linked to flexibility, emotional openness and creative adaptation were predominantly valued (73- 95% positive feelings). A third position, associated with passivity and exhaustion, elicited predominantly negative emotions (85%) while generating the highest levels of self-reflection; facilitated discussion enabled participants to acknowledge these aversive reactions and reframe them, supporting more nuanced interpretations of vulnerability in care relationships. Carefully guided engagement with a metaphor-rich picture book can help practitioners confront uncomfortable emotional reactions and re-examine implicit norms of care in emotionally demanding settings.
